headline: The framework's source carries the comments a reader can check against the code, and nothing else
summary: 60,383 comments come out of `lib/`, about 19% of its lines. What went is narrative: notes about how a decision was reached, what an earlier version did, which review round changed something. A reader opening the file has no way to verify any of it, and none of it describes what the code in front of them does. What stays is what something reads — the licence header, a documentation block carrying a tag, a suppression marker a gate consumes, the note explaining why a block is deliberately empty or why a require is deferred. A new gate refuses the rest, and `b.safeBuffer.hasCrlfOrNul` replaces two hand-rolled header checks the sweep uncovered.

items.title: Narrative comments are removed from the shipped source
items.body:
`lib/` loses 60,383 comments and 66,000 lines. No behavior changes: every one of them was a comment.

What is kept is what something reads. The licence header. A `/** */` block carrying a tag — the documentation site's page for a primitive IS that block, so those are content. A suppression marker a gate consumes (`allow:`, `eslint-disable`, `c8 ignore`). The comment that is the whole body of a block, because without it `catch (e) { }` is an unexplained swallow. The note recording why a `require` is deferred, which is what the framework's own convention asks for at such a site.

What went was the rest: how a decision was arrived at, what an earlier version did instead, which round of review changed something. A reader has no way to check any of that against the file in front of them, and it doubles the length of what they are reading to get work done.

`node scripts/strip-lib-comments.js --dry-run` reports what would go; `--apply` removes it. A new check refuses a narrative comment reaching `lib/` again, and it shares its classifier with that script rather than restating it, so the sweep and the check cannot disagree about what a comment is.

items.title: `b.safeBuffer.hasCrlfOrNul`
items.body:
Detect CR, LF or NUL in a string. A header field carries all three as one class of problem: CR and LF end the field, and NUL truncates it wherever the value reaches C. Non-string input returns `false`, so the predicate chains without a pre-typecheck, exactly as `b.safeBuffer.hasCrlf` does.

It replaces the same character loop written out twice — once where a multipart part header is parsed out of a body, once where one is serialized into a body. Both refused CR, LF and NUL already; they now ask one primitive.

items.title: `b.structuredFields` and the shared lexer expose comment ranges
items.body: `commentRanges(src)` sits beside the comment stripper in the framework's test lexer and returns every comment as a start/end pair. Finding a comment is a lexing question, not a pattern-matching one: `//` appears inside string literals, regex literals and template interpolations throughout a real codebase, and a regex cannot tell those apart from a comment. Both the sweep and the check that guards it read this one answer.

items.title: Five raw time literals a blind check had been passing over
items.body:
The check that requires a duration to go through `b.constants.TIME` removed a trailing comment from each line only after it had tried to remove regex literals. On a line like `exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 300,` followed by a comment, the slash of the division and the slash opening the comment read as a pattern, so everything between them was discarded and the literal the check exists to find was never examined.

It takes comments off through the lexer now, which is what decides a regex from a division. Five durations were behind that — two in CIBA client assertions, one in the SD-JWT-VC default credential lifetime, two in the SRS day-rotation window — and each is expressed through `b.constants.TIME`. No lifetime changes value.

items.title: A narrative comment in `lib/` is refused
items.body: `testLibCarriesNoNarrativeComments` walks every file with the lexer and reports any comment outside the kept classes, naming the file and line and the command that removes them. It cannot be expressed as a pattern in the framework's regex-driven catalog, which is the reason it lives beside the other lexer-backed checks.
